passages.title: Why We Put Things Off
passages.text: Almost everyone has delayed an important task at some point, choosing to tidy a desk or check messages instead of starting an essay. For a long time, procrastination was seen simply as a problem of laziness or poor time management. More recent research, however, suggests that it has more to do with emotions than with time. According to this view, we avoid tasks that make us feel anxious, bored or insecure. Putting them off brings immediate relief, and the brain quickly learns to repeat a behaviour that makes us feel better, even if the long-term consequences are negative. This explains why simply telling a procrastinator to "manage their time better" rarely works. Psychologists now recommend strategies that reduce the emotional cost of starting. One popular technique is to commit to working on a task for just five minutes; once people begin, they often find it easier to continue. Another is to forgive yourself for past delays. In one study, students who were kind to themselves after procrastinating before a first exam were less likely to procrastinate before the next one. Perhaps the most important lesson is that procrastination is not a sign of a weak character. It is a very human response to uncomfortable feelings, and like most habits, it can be changed with patience and practice.

passages.title: The Comeback of the Bicycle
passages.text: For most of the twentieth century, city planners around the world designed streets mainly for cars. Wide roads and large car parks were seen as signs of progress, while bicycles were often considered old-fashioned or dangerous. In recent decades, however, many cities have begun to change direction. Faced with traffic jams, air pollution and rising rates of heart disease, they have started to build protected cycle lanes, introduce bike-sharing schemes and reduce speed limits in central areas. The results have often been striking. Where safe routes have been created, the number of people cycling has usually risen quickly, including groups who rarely cycled before, such as older people and parents with children. Local shops have frequently benefited too, since cyclists tend to stop more often than drivers. Not everyone welcomes the change. Some drivers complain that cycle lanes make traffic worse, and shop owners sometimes fear losing customers who arrive by car. Climate and geography also matter: cycling is far easier in flat, mild cities than in hot or hilly ones. Even so, the experience of many cities suggests that people's habits are not fixed. When cycling becomes safe and convenient, a surprising number of people are willing to leave their cars at home.
